narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 52.4% chance that you would not pass the bar exam on the first attempt. This means that, based on your academic record, you were viewed as slightly more likely to fail than to pass—a risk the law school was not willing to take.

The most influential factor was your class ranking. You finished in the top decile in your third year, which is much stronger than the typical accepted applicant, whose average ranking is around the sixth decile. This strong performance pushed strongly toward passing and helped your case. However, two other factors more than offset that advantage and moved the prediction toward failure.

Your first-year ranking, also in the top decile, likewise pointed toward success, but it had less influence than your third-year ranking. The deciding factor was your LSAT score. Although your score of 39 was slightly above the average for accepted students (37.18), the model treated it as the second most important signal—and it pushed toward bar exam failure. Test performance apparently weighed heavily in the prediction, and your LSAT score was not high enough to compensate for the pattern the model saw.

Taken together, your strong class positions were not enough to overcome the risk signaled by your LSAT score. To strengthen a future application, I recommend retaking the LSAT to achieve a more competitive score, and explaining in your personal statement what your high class ranks reveal about your dedication and growth.
